title: Evaluating soil erosion and runoff dynamics in a humid subtopic, low stream order, southern plains watershed from cultivation and solar farm development
abstract: Much has been done to improve soil and water conservation where agriculture has driven land use intensification. Less is known about soil- and water-related impacts from intensification driven by solar farming, especially at watershed-scales. Here we employed Hydrologic Engineering Center’s Hydrologic Modeling System (HEC-HMS) to model Pond Creek, a rural watershed in Texas, USA. Land use is primarily crop cultivation and secondarily pasture for cattle grazing. Presently, several industrial-scale projects are planned to convert ≈15-30% of Pond Creek from agriculture to solar farms. The model was parameterized using public data sources (USDA, USGS) and information from local stakeholders, then calibrated to several historical precipitation events. Experiments were conducted by varying precipitation depth, duration, and land uses: native vegetation pre-cultivation (control), current cultivated conditions (current), current conditions with 15% solar farm conversion (solar), and current conditions with 30% solar farm conversion (solar x2). Cumulative sediment load significantly increased when land shifted from current to solar or solar x2 treatments, although peak discharge rate differences were not significant. Comparison to soil loss tolerance values showed current and solar treatment erosion rates exceed inferred soil generation rates. All treatments were significantly different from the native control, illustrating long-term shifts in watershed functions. We discuss high leverage strategies likely applicable to solar farm sites as well as whole watersheds where they reside. With accelerated demand for rural solar farm development, greater attention is warranted from the soil and water conservation community to better prepare for the impacts such changes will have across working landscapes.

- 36 **1. Introduction**

- 37 Land is being used with increasing intensity in order to meet the growing needs of the

- 38 human population (Tillman et al., 2002). The sustainability of land use over time, however,

- 39 depends on the ability of land resources to continue delivering ecosystem goods and

- 40 services for both current and future generations. Unfortunately, in many regions around

- 41 the world, intensification is occurring at a rate beyond what ecosystems can support

- 42 (Tillman et al., 2011). It is for this reason that conservation of resources should be among

- 43 the top priorities of policymakers and land managers, whose decisions affect the use of 44 productive land. Soil and water-driven ecological processes are particularly central to

- 45 many ecosystem goods and services, especially in landscapes characterized by their use

- 46 for wide-scale agricultural production (Montgomery, 2007).

- 47 The toll which poor management practices or land management decisions take on

- 48 the soil can hardly be appreciated in the short term. Fertile topsoil eroded out of the 49 landscape is a finite resource that cannot be regenerated in the short term if exhausted.

- 50 Approximately 0.04 inches of soil are lost every year to erosion worldwide (Montgomery,

- 51 2007). On average, it takes about 500 years to regenerate a single inch of topsoil;

- 52 degradation is virtually irreversible in the long-term (Montgomery, 2007). Water runoff is

- 53 one of several mechanisms which contribute to erosion over time. Water runoff is itself

- 54 influenced by vegetative cover across the landscape as well as current and previous soil

- 55 disturbances (e.g., grazing, crop cultivation, logging, mining, etc.; Foster et al. 2003;

- 56 Monger et al. 2015; Turner et al. 2018a, Turner et al. 2018b). Modifications in vegetation

- 57 cover and disturbances caused by different land uses are critical factors in both runoff

- 58 generation and soil erosion processes (Grismer, et al., 2005).

59 Erosion caused by raindrop impact and associated runoff is detrimental to

- 60 agricultural production as it consumes the capacity of land to grow crops (Kinnell, 2016).

- 61 Its problematic effects are augmented when land is utilized for purposes which make it

- 62 more prone to runoff (e.g., land cultivated without regard to soil conservation practices).

- 63 A natural cover from native vegetation and deep-rooted plants protect soil against

- 64 erosion, while soil exposure (e.g., plowing or overgrazing) leaves soil particles prone to

- 65 detachment. Land cover also influences the infiltration of water into soils. For example, in

- 66 cropping systems, row spacing leaves some ground bare, leading to the soil exposure to 67 wind, water and raindrop impact. Many economically significant crops are annual species

- 68 (e.g., corn, soybeans, wheat, oats) or perennials managed as annuals (e.g., cotton). This

- 69 leads to temporally inactive root growth zone during non-growing seasons which

- 70 influences the state of the soil profile. Factors such as these enhance the force of raindrop

- 71 impact to the soil surface and resulting displacement of sediment particles (Kinnell, 2009).

- 72 For example, precipitation that would have normally infiltrated and stored in a soil with 73 adequate surface cover, rooting activity, and subsurface soil aggregation, will runoff and

- 74 carry more sediment and infiltrate less water when land is converted to uses leading to

- 75 inadequate soil cover and subsurface aggregation. Sustainable land and watershed

- 76 management principles exist (Whisenant 1999; Heathcote 2009; Brooks et al. 2012), but

- 77 need to be contextualized to efficiently mitigate these effects so that soil and hydrologic

- 78 processes do not lose function as intensification continues (Tilman et al 2002; 2011).

- 79 Considerable effort has been made to minimize soil disturbance originating from

- 80 agriculture and grazing (Grismer, 2007). In developed countries, conservation farming

- 81 has emerged as a means to maintain high crop yields without disturbing the soil.

- 82 Intensively managed grazing allows for land rotations that enable grasslands to replenish

- 83 their productive capacity (Foley et al., 2011; Teague et al. 2011; Teague and Kreuter

- 84 2020). Although much work has been done in agricultural settings, questions remain

- 85 about the potential soil consequences caused by land conversion for alternative energy

- 86 development such as wind or solar farms, and the long-term implication on soil functions 87 central to ecosystem goods and services delivery (Cook et al., 2013).

- 88 The desire for clean energy has become more prominent over the past decade; 89 especially in developed nations. With various efforts to achieve “clean” or “green” energy

- 90 systems approaches, solar farms have become a major investment for organizations, 91 businesses, and cities with the goal of diluting anthropogenic carbon footprints. Solar 92 energy investment is attractive to many, given the lucrative financial incentives such as 93 federal subsidies (U.S. Department of Agriculture 2022) and tax credits at the state level

- 94 (U.S. Department of Energy 2021). Though these new “clean” or “green” forms of energy

- 95 may help reduce carbon energy consumption, the full range of ecological impacts and 96 tradeoffs have not been thoroughly assessed (Cook, et al., 2013).

- 97 The purpose of this study was to develop and describe a watershed model of Pond

- 98 Creek, Texas, USA, used to evaluate watershed discharge (or flow leaving the 99 watershed) and erosion (measured in cumulative sediment loading) in response to

- 100 varying land uses and precipitation treatments. The model was developed in HEC-HMS

- 101 (Chu et al., 2009; Hydrologic Engineering Center 2022) and calibrated using variety of

- 102 data sources including National Cooperative Soil Survey, USDA National Agricultural

- 103 Statistics Service Cropland Data Layer and USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service

- 104 survey data accessed via Quick Stats. Of secondary interest was the comparison of

- 105 sediment losses in the watershed to soil loss tolerance values (T-values). Soil loss

- 106 tolerance is commonly defined as the maximum acceptable annual soil loss capable of

- 107 permitting and maintain aboveground productivity economically and indefinitely

- 108 (Wischmeier and Smith 1978; see Li et al. 2009 for other considerations) and has 109 historically been used for conservation planning and evaluation (Alewell et al. 2019).

- 110 This paper overviews the model and its application to assess soil and hydrologic

- 111 effects of large-scale solar energy projects. By using a model, we aimed to better

- 112 understand the interaction between land use change as a result of solar energy

- 113 development with a watershed’s inherent soil properties, such as erodibility, slope, and

- 114 surface cover, and hydrologic behaviors such as peak discharge and cumulative runoff

- 115 and sediment load volumes. Insights are discussed regarding the implications of solar

- 116 farms on soil conservation on site, on land adjacent to them, and in watersheds in which 117 they reside.

- 118 **2. Methods**

- 119 _2.1. Study area and relevant background data_

- 120 The Pond Creek watershed is made up of two contributing creeks: Big Pond Creek and

- 121 Little Pond Creek (Figure 1). Big Pond Creek originates north of Westphalia, Texas and

- 122 flows southeast approximately 35 miles (56.3 km) from Bell to Falls and Milam counties

- 123 where its empties into the Brazos River north of Calvert, Texas. Little Pond Creek

- 124 originates south of Westphalia and flows through Falls and Milam counties approximately

- 125 25 miles (40.2 km) before it empties into Big Pond Creek 12 miles (19.3 km) above the

- 126 Brazos River conveyance. The watershed is subdivided into five sub catchments at the

- 127 U.S. Geologic Survey (USGS) hydrologic unit code (HUC) 12 classification 128 (120701010401 to 120701010405 in the Lower Brazos River; USGS 2013).

- 129 The land composition in the north of Pond Creek watershed is moderately rolling,

- 130 where short low order tributary reaches (orders one to two) drain cultivated agricultural 131 land. In the central to southern region, short, linear to slightly meandering channels with

- 132 intermittent flows can be observed. The southern part of the watershed is also rolling, but

- 133 with longer, narrower intermittent tributary reaches (orders two to three) on the north side 134 and short tributary reaches (orders one to one) originating form moderately to steeply 135 rolling hills on the south side. Longer, meandering reaches and perennial flows can be 136 observed at the bottom of the watershed (VanZandt 1973). The geopolitical boundaries 137 relevant to this study include Falls, Bell, and Milam Counties, which have undergone a

- 138 significant shift in agricultural land use over time (USDA National Agricultural Statistics 139 Service 2021; Figure 2).

- 140 Soils in Pond Creek watershed are predominately characterized by soil profiles 141 identified as Burleson, Heiden, Houston Black clays (Fine, smectitic, thermic Udic 142 Haplusterts), Wilson loam and Wilson silty clay loam (Fine, smectitic, thermic Oxyaquic 143 Vertic Haplustalfs), and Crockett fine land loams (Fine, smectitic, thermic Udertic

- 144 Paleustalfs; USDA National Cooperative Soil Survey Staff 2017). The entirety of Pond 145 Creek watershed resides in the Blackland prairie and Post Oak savanah ecoregions of

- 146 Texas (Gould 1975) on the south eastern edge of the Great Plains, North America.

- 147 Climate within the Pond Creek watershed is humid subtropic exhibiting a mean

- 148 annual temperature of 20.3°C (68.5°F), varying to 10.7°C (51.3°F) in winter and 29°C 149 (84.2°F) in the summer (WeatherWX 2022). Annual temperature varies from 4.4°C (40°F)

- 150 to 36.1°C (97°F) and is rarely below -2.2°C (28°F) or above 38.9°C (102°F). Precipitation

- 151 varies seasonally, with highest levels between October and June (4 inches or 10.6 cm),

- 152 and lows between the end of June and the beginning of October (1.5 inches or 3.81 cm)

- 153 with an annual average precipitation of 36 inches (91.4 cm; Weatherspark 2022).

- 154 For the purposes of this study, both USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service 155 (NASS) annual survey data as well as Cropland Data Layer’s (CDL) land use information 156 was consulted and recorded for five sub watersheds that make up the Pond Creek

- 157 Watershed and the three counties it resides in (USDA NASS CDL 2021). The most recent

- 158 CDL year, 2020, was used for model development to reflect most recent conditions,

- 159 whereas survey data from the early 1970s was used for model calibration (described

- 160 below). The primary crops identified were corn ( _Zea mays_ ), winter wheat ( _Triticum_

- 161 _aestivum_ L.), oats ( _Avena sativa_ ), and hay and pasture for grazing, primarily beef cattle

- 162 (both _Bos tarus_ and _Bos indicus_ ).

- 163 _2.2. HEC-HMS model development_

- 164 The _Hydrologic Engineering Center–Hydrologic Modeling System_ (HEC-HMS) version

- 165 4.0 is a program which enables the user to simulate hydrologic processes such as water

- 166 runoff, sediment transcript, and reservoir routing in branched water systems (Pak, et al.,

- 167 2015; Hydrologic Engineering Center 2022). The HEC-HMS program estimates 168 watershed runoff, surface erosion, and sediment loading from both single rainfall events

- 169 (i.e., discrete events) or long-term precipitation data (i.e., for continuous simulation). The 170 HEC-HMS simulation architecture employs well established hydrologic and soil modeling

- 171 frameworks, such as the Modified Universal Soil Loss Equation (MUSLE; Williams, 1975).

- 172 This equation is widely applied globally for its simplicity and versatility (Alewell et al. 173 2019).

- 174 In the following sections, we describe in more technical detail how the model was

- 175 constructed, information and data sources used for parametrization, and the model

- 176 evaluation and calibration process supported by observed historical data (conceptualized

- 177 in Figure 3).

- 178 _2.2.1. Reach organization and flow routing_

- 179 The watershed area and its subwatersheds were imported to HEC-HMS via shape files

- 180 of the five USGS HUC 12 sub watersheds that make up the Pond Creek system.

- 181 Parametrization of each subwatershed required the following inputs (summarized in Table

- 182 1): selection of canopy, loss, transformation, baseflow, and reach routing method. Canopy

- 183 method selection represents plants being present in the landscape, and accounts for

- 184 precipitation interception and soil water extraction through evapotranspiration (Hydrologic 185 Engineering Center 2022). The loss rate partitions precipitation into either infiltration or

- 186 runoff excess (XMS Wiki, 2016). Transformation method is the component which carries

- 187

- 188 (HMS User’s manual 2021). Baseflow method accounts for the portion of the stream

- 189 which does not originate from runoff, but rather from the ground into the channel with a

- 190 certain time delay (Freie Universität Berlin, 2014). Reach routing method estimates

- 191 changes in the shape of the runoff hydrograph within each reach element of the model 192 (Hydrologic Engineering Center 2022).

- 193 _2.2.2. Sediment generation_

- 194 The USDA Web Soil Survey was utilized to collect the required sol data that would allow

- 195 estimation of sediment transport. Parametrization of each subwatershed’s sediment

- 196 generation required the following inputs (Table 2): selection of erosion and fall velocity

- 197 method, erodibility, topographic, practice, cover, exponent, and threshold factors. The

- 198 erosion method serves to compute the sediment load that is transported out of a 199 subwatershed during the duration of a precipitation event. Sediment distribution is

- 200 illustrated in a time-series of sediment discharge (Hydrologic Engineering Center 2022).

- 201 The fall velocity method is used to determine the transport of the sediment particles 202 suspended in water (Hydrologic Engineering Center 2022). Erodibility (K), topography 203 (LS), cover management (C), practice factors (P) are used as part of the Modified 204 Universal Soil Loss Equation employed by HEC-HMS for calculating sediment 205 displacement (Williams, 1975). The soil erodibility factor accounts for the capacity of the

- 206 soil to resist erosion. The topographic factor contributes in defining the capacity of the

- 207 terrain to exert erosive force due to field length, field slope and runoff accumulation. The

- 208 cover factor identifies the effect of vegetation on soil erosion. Data on the amount of cover

- 209 and type of cover in the area were needed as inputs. Practice factor serves to represent

- 210 the impact of different management practices, such as types of agriculture or urban

- 211 development (Acosta et al., 2019; Michigan State University Institute for Water Research 212 2002).

- 213 A number of parameter values had to be obtained in order to meet the minimum 214 requirements needed for soil erosion (particularly Universal Soil Loss Equation or USLE

- 215 factors) and sediment transport estimation. They were needed in order to estimate the

- 216 erosion rate in the soil surface, given varying land uses, topographic slope and soil

- 217 textural characteristics. To determine USLE parameter values, we identified USLE factor

- 218 values for each soil map unit in each sub watershed and then estimated a weighted 219 average value for each factor based on the proportion of the sub watershed composed of 220 each soil map unit.

- 221 Land use information was collected using the National Agricultural Statistics

- 222 Service (NASS) program CropScape (USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service 223 Cropland Data Layer, 2021) to inform parametrization of soil cover factors. A similar 224 weighted average procedure was used to calculate the value used in HEC-HMS. The 225 hydrologic soil group values for each sub watershed were found with Natural Resources 226 Conservation Service’s (NRCS) Web Soil Survey (USDA National Cooperative Soil 227 Survey Staff 2017). The K value (susceptibility of the soil to sheet and rill erosion), Slope

- 228 RV value (how much of an incline the soil has relative to the horizontal) and Length of 229 Slope were calculated from this same information.

- 230 Another component utilized for the HEC-HMS model was the Soil Curve Number

- 231 (CN). This parameter describes the runoff potential of the drainage area in question. In

- 232 this case the CN was calculated by utilizing the values from USDA CropScape (USDA 233 NASS CDL 2021) and obtaining the acreage in cultivation and of native vegetation as a

- 234 percentage of the total area of each sub watershed. A curve number was then derived for 235 every subwatershed after dividing the cultivated percentages by the ratio which had poor

- 236 crop residue and adding the outcome to the result of the division of native vegetation by 237 the fraction that is suitable for grazing.

- 238 _2.3 Model simulation, calibration and experimental design_

## 239 _2.3.1 Initial Simulation_

- 240 HEC-HMS requires an input of at least one precipitation event in order to conduct a

- 241 simulation. Various events were utilized for the purpose of this experiment (described

- 242 below) after parameterization and simulation of a 2-inch (5.08 cm), 6-hour precipitation

- 243 event to scrutinize the model for errors. Precipitation unit for HEC-HMS was millimeters 244 per hour and the event was applied to all five subwatersheds simultaneously.

- 245 In HEC-HMS, each sub watershed was organized and interconnected via junctions

- 246 and reaches. Subdivisions were manually placed on the Pond Creek and linked to each

- 247 other within the model to direct the route and direction of the flow, as well as its point of

- 248 discharge out of the watershed. As mentioned previously, the sub catchments and reach

- 249 components required inputs and selection of calculation methods (Tables 1 and Table 2)

- 250 in order to execute a simulation. Initial simulations provided feasible and reasonable 251 results, leading us to proceed into a formal model calibration phase.

- 252 _2.3.2 Calibration_

- 253 For the purposes of model calibration, a fraction of sub watershed 404 was used to match

- 254 the contributing area above the USGS monitoring location on Little Pond Creek during

- 255 the Small Watershed Project completed in 1970s (Figure 1). After refinements for model

- 256 calibration, the discharge from sub watershed 405 was used to compare discharge and

- 257 sediment load changes from varying land use scenarios.

- 258 The process of calibration took place in order to ensure that the fully parameterized

- 259 model would accurately and reliably illustrate the effects of land use and intensity of

- 260 rainfall on soil and water runoff. Given Pond Creek is an ungauged watershed, no known

- 261 contemporary dataset exists to be able to calibrate the model to currently observed

- 262 watershed conditions. In the 1970s, however, the USGS did monitor the northern half of

- 263 Little Pond Creek above Burlington, Texas, as part of a nationwide Small Watershed 264 Project (Figure 1; VanZandt 1973), providing three unique precipitation and runoff events

- 265 which occurred in 1971 in which to calibrate HEC-HMS model outputs to some historically

- 266 observed events.

- 270 county level, we estimated the cultivated land area in Pond Creek using the approximate

- 272 fractions of land in cultivation. This cultivated land area estimate was then used to revise 273 soil curve numbers and USLE factors using a similar weighted average procedure

- 274 described above. Finally, because the USGS’s monitoring point resided in the middle of

- 275 Little Pond Creek, the HEC-HMS output for sub watershed 404 (Figure 1) was multiplied

- 276 by the estimated fraction of total watershed runoff captured at the monitoring point,

- 282 _2.3.3 Experimental design_

- 317 With the experimental simulations defined, we sought to test the following 318 hypotheses:

- 319 • H0: There is no significant difference in peak discharge and sediment load 320 rates or cumulative discharge and sediment load volumes between current 321 land uses with or without solar panels.

- 322 • Ha: The peak discharge and sediment load rates or cumulative discharge 323 and sediment load volumes are significantly greater under land use 324 conditions after solar panel installation.

- 325 Determination of significance between the current peak discharge rates and sediment 326 load volumes and those of the solar panel treatments was made by calculating the

- 327 percentage differences in these values. If the percentage differences between current 328 and solar panel treatments exceeded the error percentages obtained in model calibration,

## 342 **3. Results**

- 343 _3.1. Model calibration to historical precipitation and runoff events_

- 344 The historical data provided in the USGS Small Watershed Project study (VanZandt

- 345 1973) included three unique precipitation events: (a) 1.5-inch (4 cm) 12-hour storm, (b)

- 346 3.1-inch (7.9 cm) 3-hour storm, (c) and 0.9-inch (2.3 cm) 6-hour storm, which were input

- 347 into the HEC-HMS model under 1970 land use and management conditions. Results of

- 348 the modeled discharge approximated for the USGS site were compared to observed

- 349 discharge at that location (Figure 4, panels a, b, and c correspond to precipitation events

- 350 a, b, and c listed above). The model yielded a mean coefficient of determination value of

- 351 0.44 (ranging from 0.24 to 0.81), mean estimates of mean bias (MB) of 9% (ranging from

- 352 -23% to 45%), mean differences in peak discharge rates of -4.5 cubic meters per second

- 353 (ranging from -0.3 to -11.5), mean difference in peak discharge rates on a percentage

- 354 basis of 10.7% (ranging from 4 to 16%), and a mean difference in peak discharge time of 355 2.67 hours (ranging from 0 to 6 hours).

- 356 Calibration estimates for model accuracy were used to determine significance of

- 357 treatments. Although these model calibration measurements were not tightly correlated

- 358 to the observed data (discussed below), the trade-off was that it would be more difficult

- 359 to find statistical significance in watershed changes due to solar panel treatments given

- 360 the level of change that would need to occur to offset or overcome the initial model

- 361 accuracy (i.e., greater accuracy of model performance is more likely to detect significance

- 362 in simulation treatments). If the percentage change in peak discharge rate of the solar

- 363 panel treatment from the current watershed simulation output exceeded 10.7%, that

- 364 treatment was determined significant, otherwise we state no statistically observable

- 365 difference given the inherent accuracy of the model. Similarly, if the percentage change

- 366 in sediment load of the solar panel treatment from the current watershed simulation output

- 367 exceeded 9%, the mean bias of the total discharge, that treatment was determined

- 368 significant, otherwise we state no statistically observable difference given the inherent 369 accuracy of the model.

- 370 _3.2. Model experiments: watershed responses to varying land use, precipitation depths_ 371 _and intensity_

- 372 The control simulation results showed minimal runoff and sediment displacement in

- 373 comparison to the rest of the experimental simulations, the lowest out of the four

- 374 simulations (Figure 5), with the latter measurement being the one exhibiting the greatest

- 375 contrast. On average, the peak outflow rates in the control were between 78.8% and

- 376 92.7% (in 2-inch events) and 11.3% and 16.5% (in 6-inch events) greater than the other

- 377 treatments (Table 4), whereas differences in cumulative sediment ranged from 26 to 61

- 378 times less than the treatments across all simulations (Table 5).

- 379 Although the current and solar panel treatments were of greater interest for the 380 purposes of this study, simulating a hypothetical native control representing the

- 381 landscape prior to crop cultivation provided another point of comparison beyond the

- 382 statistical consideration used in the remaining treatments. The current treatment

- 383 representing the existing cultivated state of the watershed resulted in mean peak

- 384 discharge values 84.9, 78.8, 15.4, and 11.3% greater than the native control (Table 4),

- 385 while cumulative sediment load exceeded the native control by 46 to 47 times or 26 to 27

- 386 times depending on precipitation depth and length of event (Table 5).

387 The first solar panel treatment, which included 15% land use conversion for solar 388 site development, increased peak discharge rates between 0.38% to 2.06% from the 389 current treatment, which was not significant (Table 4). On the other hand, cumulative 390 sediment load increased between 12.68% and 14.87%, which were significant (I.e., 391 greater than calibration measured mean bias threshold of 9%).

392 The double solar panel treatment ( _solar x2_ ), represented a 30% land use 393 conversion for solar site development. Given that the land use input was twice that of the 394 first solar panel simulations, it might be reasonable to expect that the double solar panel 395 treatment would also double the percentage change observed between the first solar 396 treatment and current conditions. Simulation results indicated a disproportionate 397 (sublinear) response in peak discharge rates given increasing levels of land conversion 398 away from the current conditions (i.e., the percentage difference from current created by 399 solar x2 were less than double the percentage change of the first solar treatment; Table 400 4). Although doubling solar panels did increase peak discharge rates (ranging from 0.73% 401 to 4.24%), these were not significant. On the other hand, doubling solar panels created a 402 disproportionate (superlinear) response in cumulative sediment load (i.e., the percentage 403 difference from current created by solar x2 were more than double the percentage change 404 of the first solar treatment; Table 5). Sediment load increased between 25.72% and 405 30.54%, all of which were significant differences relative to the current conditions.

- 406 Several overall behavioral trends were observed in the simulation results. First, 407 increasing precipitation along the gradient from 2 inches (5.08 cm) to 10 inches (25.4 cm) 408 generally lead to smaller changes in peak discharge and cumulative sediments loads 409 (Tables 4 and 5), indicating stronger influence of soil saturation effects which outweigh

- 410 other factors such as land use as precipitation increases. Second, given the inherent soil

- 411 properties (texture, porosity, hydrologic group) and average field slopes, watershed

- 412 responses in terms of runoff dynamics were less sensitive to precipitation (volume and

- 413 timing), evidenced by peak discharge results (Table 4), but were more sensitive to soil

- 414 cover type and management (Table 5). Lastly, we observed steeper slopes in the runoff

- 415 hydrograph prior to peak discharge times, slightly earlier peak discharge times for 24-

- 416 hour precipitation events, and overlap in cumulative sediment load curves under current

- 417 conditions and double solar panel treatments but under different precipitation events 418 (Figure 5).

- 420 The resulting cumulative sediment load values were used for relative comparison to soil

- 421 T-values. Pond Creek soils were assigned T-values of five tons per acre (2.023 tons per 422 hectare) per year according to USDA values (USDA National Cooperative Soil Survey

- 423 Staff 2017). Assuming uniform land use distributions consistent with HEC-HMS, mean

- 424 soil loss per unit area ranged from 0.01 to 5.84 tons per acre (0.00 to 2.36 tons per

- 425 hectare; Table 6). Mean number of treatment precipitation events needed to meet or

- 426 exceed the given T-value ranged from 0.86 to 688 (Table 6). Under two-inch precipitation

- 427 depths, T-values were not exceeded until between 8.86 events, ranging up to 15.5 events,

- 428 while 10-inch precipitation depths led to T-value exceedance in less than two (for 24-hour

- 429 storm) or less than one (for solar panel treatments in 6-hour storms). In contrast, the

- 430 number of treatment precipitation events needed to meet or exceed the T-value under the

- 431 native land use (control) simulation ranged from 30 to 688.

- 432 **4. Discussion**

- 433 As land use continues to intensify with increasing demands for food, fiber, and alternative 434 energy, both scientific evidence of environmental or ecological externalities and local

- 435 conservation concerns have grown (Foster et al. 2003; Monger et al. 2015; Turner et al. 436 2018a).  Runoff and erosion problems resulting from high intensity crop cultivation has

- 437 long been studied globally (Judson 1968; Milliman and Meade 1983; Tilman et al., 2002;

- 438 Montgomery 2007; Alewell 2019), as well as locally in Pond Creek (Turner et al. 2018b).

- 439 Known with less certainty are the implications to watersheds and local communities of 440 industrial-scale solar farm development in traditionally agricultural landscapes.

- 441 Acceleration of solar development expansion has pitted various local landowner, 442 elected official, and business or environmental special interests against each other in 443 unique ways (Groom 2022). Common concerns about the consequences of converting 444 land to solar farms include real estate and taxation implications for neighboring property, 445 erosion and runoff impacts to watershed integrity, and chemical pollution degrading water 446 quality. Several works have examined the impact of solar development on real estate 447 prices or other socioeconomic factors of interest (Al-Hamoodah et al., 2018; Gaur and 448 Lang 2020). Unfortunately, literature pertaining to solar farming development impacts on

- 449 soil, hydrologic or watershed integrity are few and far between (see Cook and McCuen

- 450 2013 for one of the few experimental examples, or Hernandez et al. 2014), but there is a 451 growing list of observational data or case study examples published in popular outlets

- 452 documenting the concerns of many diverse stakeholders (e.g., Holmberg 2018; Appel

- 453 2020; Merzbach 2020; Cohen 2021; French 2021; Patel 2022; Tuser 2022). To the best

- 454 of our knowledge, this study was one of the first to examine watershed-level impacts of

- 455 industrial-scale solar farm development in a traditionally agricultural landscape.

- 456 Our modeling results indicated non-significant increases in peak discharge due to 457 solar expansion, implying only marginal increases in watershed runoff compared to the 458 current conditions. Therefore, we failed to reject our null hypothesis as it pertained to peak 459 discharge dynamics. Despite this, simulation results did provide evidence enough to 460 reject our null hypothesis pertaining to cumulative sediment load, as model projections 461 showed a significant increase in sediment loading. Increased sediment loading without 462 significant increases in discharge implied an increase in soil loss per unit of land area. 463 This seemingly counterintuitive result appears realistic when analyzed within the context 464 of Pond Creek, which currently is already intensively cultivated, particularly in the northern 465 reaches of the watershed. Our results suggesting marginal runoff but significant sediment 466 load increases were feasible given that soil protective cover (C factor) is already sparse 467 and the management practices that enhance its effectiveness against erosion (P factor) 468 are minimal at best at a watershed scale (noted by the comparison between the current 469 condition simulation and the native control). The impact on solar expansion on C and P 470 values did not apparently cross any threshold or “tipping point” needed to significantly 471 alter the discharge dynamics, but did for erosivity given greater soil exposure and 472 accumulated surface energy from runoff capable of suspending a greater volume of soil.

- 473 In the recent past, Pond Creek has been experiencing less frequent but more 474 severe flow patterns (i.e., longer periods of time of low or no flows followed by extreme 475 flow events well above bank full flow even after small- to moderate precipitation events,

- 476 Figure 6; Anonymous landowners, personal communication, 2022). Solar panel 477 installations are likely to exacerbate this flow pattern given the nonlinear response in 478 model simulations. For example, peak discharge in the current condition simulation

479 increased 8.20 times when moving from a two inch to 10-inch 6-hr precipitation event 480 (662 to 5,428 m[3] per second). Under the solar panel conditions, the peak discharge rates 481 increased 8.07 times (676 to 5,455 m[3] per second) and 7.94 times (690 to 5480 m[3] per 482 second), respectively. Similarly, cumulative sediment load increased 10.73 times under

483 current conditions (63,428 to 681,146 tons), compared to 10.54 times (72,862 to 768,087 484 tons) and 10.35 times (82,796 to 857,522 tons) under the solar panel treatments when 485 moving from two inch to 10-inch precipitation events. The congruence of these rates and 486 volumes as precipitation increases points to potential loss of watershed function in 487 regulating infiltration-excess runoff processes given the similarity between low (2 inch) 488 and high (10 inch) precipitation rates.

489 Comparisons of simulated precipitation treatments pointed to another change in 490 watershed function in response to land use change and precipitation intensity. Infiltration 491 and soil storage capacity, capacities which are useful for dampening the slope of the 492 runoff hydrograph (i.e., lower and later peak discharge times and rates and reduced 493 cumulative runoff and sediment loading), were reduced in the current conditions and each 494 solar panel treatments as precipitation depth increased with a static storm duration. 495 However, all of current land use and projected solar panel scenarios were significantly 496 different than the peak discharge and cumulative sediment load under the native control 497 situation (evidenced by the extreme departures). This dramatic difference between an 498 assumed native (or restored watershed condition to full vegetative cover) and current 499 conditions dominated by row crop cultivation illustrates that watershed functions altered 500 by solar farm development are augmenting already existing impairments in Pond Creek 501 watershed.

502 A common interest in watershed modeling with USLE to estimate erosion and it’s

- 503 contribution to sediment loading in streams has been to compare soil erosion rates to soil

- 504 loss tolerance (T-values) and assess possible combinations for management (Alewell et 505 al. 2019).  When examining sediment losses in relation to the USDA T-value assigned to

- 506 soils in Pond Creek (5 tons per acre or 2.023 tons per hectare), we observed noteworthy

- 507 reductions in the number of treatment events needed to meet or exceed the T-value. In 508 the two-inch precipitation depths, solar panel treatments reduced the number of events 509 need to reach the T-value by 12.9% (solar to current) and 23.4% (solar x2 to current), but 510 even with these reductions the number of events at the two-inch depth are consistent with 511 realistic and feasible potential precipitation given the long-term annual average 512 precipitation received (≈36 inches or 91.4 cm). As precipitation depths increased to 10513 inches (25.4 cm), the number of events needed for soil loss to meet the T-value were 514 reduced by 11.3% to 20.6%, and in some cases sediment removal exceeded the T-value 515 in less than one precipitation event. The native control simulation, by comparison, needed 516 between 30 and 688 treatment precipitation events (or roughly 10 times the current long517 term annual mean) in order for meet the assigned T-value.

- 518 These estimates likewise point to Pond Creek being an already highly altered 519 watershed that is likely to become even less resilient in the face of climate changes given

- 520 the clear reduction in discharge capacity with the presence of solar panels. The erosion

- 521 rates estimated here were clearly above the natural soil formation rate (note the 522 differences between soil loss estimates in native control compared to all other treatments)

- 523 and consistent with rates reported in Montgomery (2007). Comparison of sediment losses

- 524 to USDA T-values should be appropriately weighed,  however, given the problems of

- 525 scaling (see Verheijen et al. 2009) as well as model accounting for sedimentation in 526 stream channel prior to discharging from the watershed (i.e., eroded soil which has 527 escaped the field but settles in the stream channel as discharge rate slows  leads to 528 underestimation of soil erosion per unit area when relying on cumulative sediment losses

- 529 downstream out of a watershed; see discussions in Montgomery 2007 and Verheijen et 530 al. 2009 for additional discussion about erosion modeling scale and interpretation).

- 531 Collectively, these point to several potential leverage points or best management 532 practices that would improve hydrologic function and soil conversation in Pond Creek 533 watershed. First, investment in ecological restoration surrounding solar farm 534 development, thereby improving the cover, C, and practice, P, factors (e.g., buffer strips 535 surrounding solar farm boundaries, grassed waterways across hillslope contours, etc.),

- 536 has the potential to reduce soil runoff and erosion impacts induced by solar farm 537 manipulation such that the net impact is consistent with existing runoff and erosion given 538 current land uses, in this case crop cultivation. In regions of more humid environments,

- 539 regions that do not rely on crop cultivation due to soil limitations, and where soil is 540 naturally covered with vegetation throughout the year, solar farm development is likely to 541 lead to even larger increases in peak discharge and cumulative sediment loading than 542 estimated here given the more severe land use disturbance that occurs relative to the 543 existing ecosystem. In such cases, in-situ soil protection via vegetation restoration and

- 544 management will be critical on and immediately surrounding solar farms, while 545 streambank conservation measures may be added or enhanced downstream to bolster

- 546 channel integrity and watershed function (e.g., brush layering or woody debris, cross-

- 547 vaning, rip rap, log vanes, mulch planting, etc.). In more arid environments that likewise

- 548 have soil limitations but receive less total annual precipitation in short, flashy rainy 549 seasons, vegetation management will not be effective conservation measures in and

- 550 around solar farm developments without other environmental trade-offs (e.g., irrigation

- 551 water requirements to support added vegetation). Therefore, placement of solar farms

- 552 may be more critical so that panel networks and other critical infrastructure respect slope

- 553 and topography and existing land uses (including critical habitat) to minimize potential

- 554 impact on plant and animal populations and as well as interactions with or damage from

- 555 arroyo networks, which are shaped and evolved by precipitation patterns (see Mokarram 556 et al. 2020 who developed a multi-criteria decision methodology for solar farm placement

- 557 determination).

- 558 The second leverage point or insight pertaining to Pond Creek is that, given the 559 current land use conditions, any revitalized (e.g., terracing and contour planting) or new

- 560 (e.g., multispecies cover cropping, livestock-integration) conservation practices will have 561 disproportionately positive impacts on watershed functions and therefore runoff and

- 562 erosion dynamics. If existing cost-share programs or other conservation funding 563 mechanisms are inadequate to offset the costs of implementing such practices, local

- 564 institutions or policy makers interacting with solar project developers should seek 565 requiring investments by energy developers to assist in watershed conservation 566 measures. Doing so would lead to improved watershed functions post-solar farm

- 567 installation in the best case, or maintain existing watershed functions post-solar farm

- 568 installation in the worst case.

- 569 _4.1. Model contributions, strengths, limitations, and future directions_

- 570 The main contribution of this work was that it was one of the first efforts we are aware of

- 571 to quantify soil- and water-related impacts of solar energy development at watershed

- 572 scales, which is critically important given the pace of development in alternative energy

- 573 projects such as solar farms across agricultural lands used for crop and livestock

- 574 production. Although imperfect like all models, it provides a baseline from which future

- 575 environmental assessments can improve upon for evaluating land use change in

- 576 response to novel uses such as solar farming. The strength of the model, representing a

- 577 currently ungauged watershed, was the ability to calibrate to a sample of historic data to

- 578 quantitatively evaluate the and provide a basis for significance testing. This was important

- 579 given that HEC-HMS is a deterministic model where we readily mentally intuit the 580 direction and magnitude of changes (both small and large) in model output behavior as a

- 581 result of changes in the input parameters. Without historical data by which to compare,

- 582 results from HEC-HMS simulations such as those completed here would only confirm our

- 583 intuition about changes in runoff and soil sediment loading given changes in input 584 parameters such as cover, C, and practice, P, factor values or curve number (CN) values 585 resulting from land use changes driven by solar farming. Although not a perfect

- 586 calibration, which generally isn’t feasible or cost effective for nearly any modeling project,

- 587 the calibration provided a baseline from which to evaluate changes.

- 588 On the other hand, the availability of historic data did limit the information needed

- 589 to better refine the model and produce behaviors more consistent with the observed

- 590 precipitation events, a statistical weakness that potentially may point towards structural

- 591 weaknesses in the parameterization if further refinement were possible. One of the 592 challenges in this particular case was that the precipitation values input in the model

- 593 representing in USGS (VanZandt 1973) were a composite of three different precipitation 594 gauges in the northern reaches of subwatershed 404 which illustrated extreme variation 595 in precipitation depths and timing, even for the same event. This resulted in good 596 calibration performance for simple and uniformly distributed precipitation events (such as

- 597 panel a in Figure 4), but the more complex the precipitation event (i.e., discontinuously 598 timed and unequal depths) the more difficult it was to calibrate and generally made 599 calibration estimates weaker (panel c in Figure 4) given the manner in which HEC-HMS 600 applies precipitation events to the entire watershed or subwatershed it is assigned to. 601 Without higher resolution land use information, parameterizing HEC-HMS to a finer level 602 and therefore being able to capture these gauges independently was not possible.

- 603 It is also worth noting the well documented strengths (flexibility, data accessibility, 604 parsimonious structure, extensive literature and comparability of results) and weaknesses 605 (lacks accounting for soil deposition, lacks measured data to rigorously determine all 606 factors needed for most situations) of the USLE framework for erosion (Wischmeier and 607 Smith 1965; 1978). Depending on data availability and model purpose, alternative 608 simulation frameworks or interfaces such as Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), 609 Watershed Erosion Prediction Project (WEPP), SIMulated Water Erosion (SIMWE), 610 among others, may be more or less appropriate (Mitasova and Mitas 2001). In addition, 611 the combination of runoff modeling coupled to USLE erosion modeling for watershed612 level studies must be interpreted carefully given scaling effects don’t accurately reflect 613 true soil loss due to sediment deposition in channels (Judson 1968; Milliman and Meade 614 1983) as well as scale-dependent effects in erosion estimates (Pierson et al. 1994; Van

- 615 Noordwijk et al. 1998). More interested readers are encouraged to consult Alewell et al. 616 (2019) for more details about these erosion modeling considerations.

- 617 Future work could include some short-term monitoring to gauge Pond Creek and

- 618 provide an up-to-date database in which to calibrate to, land use assessments using

- 619 historical imagery to be able model the watershed at a higher resolution, and assessment

- 620 of watershed responses to extreme events (similar to Turner et al 2018b) which may

- 621 inform the model for updated calibrations if no other data are available.

- 622 **5. Conclusion**

- 623 Land use intensity is expected to grow in order to meet increasingly diverse societal 624 needs. These include crop production for food and fiber as well as alternative energy

- 625 development such as solar farming. Without proactive conservation policy efforts or

- 626 investment, greater attention to and management of soil and water conservation to protect

- 627 and sustain the healthy functioning of watersheds will be critical. Although much work has 628 been done in watersheds where crop cultivation is a significant land use driver,

- 629 information pertaining to the impacts of industrial solar farm development in rural 630 watersheds remains sparser.

- 631 Here we used HEC–HMS to estimate runoff and sediment load from varying 632 precipitation events and land use patterns in the Pond Creek watershed, Texas, USA, an 633 ungauged small order stream system contributing to the Brazos River. The model was

- 634 developed from best available data from a variety of sources, including USDA NASS, 635 USDA Soil Survey, and first-hand knowledge of the watershed provided by stakeholders.

- 636 Following a calibration procedure whereby model performance was evaluated against

- 637 three historical precipitation events recorded by the USGS, the model was tested for a

- 638 variety of precipitation events and land use conditions (native, current cultivation

- 639 conditions, and current cultivation conditions with solar farm development) to observe

- 640 changes in discharge (m[3] per second) and cumulative sediment load (tons).  Results

- 641 indicated that although increases in peak discharge rate between current and solar panel

- 642 treatments were marginal and statistically insignificant, increases in cumulative sediment

- 643 loading due to alteration of soil surface cover and management were statistically 644 significant.

- 645 Similar HEC–HMS models for watershed discharge and sediment loading (or other

- 646 similar frameworks) can be applied to other watersheds experiencing more rapid land use

- 647 intensification with the onset alternative energy investments such as solar farms. The

- 648 Pond Creek watershed modeled here is an agriculturally-driven watershed which may or

- 649 may not be representative of other watersheds in Texas or the United States at-large,

- 650 given the diversity of soils, climates, and socioeconomic factors involved. This application

- 651 does however provide an initial framework for identifying and harnessing unique sets of

- 652 data for modeling purposes which are prospective looking in nature in order to evaluate

- 653 rapidly emerging land use concerns such as solar development.
